content.p: In the first days of August 2014, fighters of the Islamic State overran Sinjar, a district in northwestern Iraq where most of the world's Yazidis lived. What followed was a flight, a siege and a series of killings and abductions that the United Nations documented within weeks. Tens of thousands of civilians ran to the bare slopes of Mount Sinjar, where they were surrounded in summer heat with little food or water. Men were shot in villages and on roads, and women and children were taken away. It was the opening of a campaign against the Yazidi community that drew the United States back into air operations over Iraq.

The figures in this account come from different people, and they do not agree. Where a number is given, the text says who gave it. The group's responsibility is described as the UN, journalists and Iraqi officials reported it; no court verdict is among the pages used here.
content.h2: A people living in one place
content.p: Yazidis follow a religion that Al Jazeera described as older than Islam and Christianity, rooted in Mesopotamia. Most of them lived in Nineveh province, in places such as Sinjar, Shekhan and Bashiqa, and most spoke the Kurmanji dialect of Kurdish. The BBC put their worldwide number at around 500,000. Many Muslims wrongly call them devil worshippers, the BBC noted. Islamic State fighters regarded them as non-believers, in the words of the UN report, and offered them a choice between conversion and death.

Violence against them was not new. In August 2007, coordinated attacks on villages near Sinjar killed around 500 Yazidis, according to Al Jazeera; the BBC gave a range of 400 to 700. The head of the Shekhan municipality, Mamo Selim al-Bagsri, told Al Jazeera in 2014 that around 85 percent of the Yazidis lived in Sinjar, and he warned that mass killing there would have an irreversible effect on the community.

The Islamic State had been taking ground in northern Iraq since June 2014, the BBC reported, and held part of Syria as well. On Sunday 3 August its fighters took the Sinjar area. Khalaf Qassim, a former member of the security forces from Bari village on the Syrian border, told Al Jazeera that he and his neighbours left at once. He showed the reporter a text message he said had come from an IS member, threatening to cut him into pieces and asking why he had not come to repent.

Many residents were angry at the Kurdish Peshmerga forces, who they said had not resisted. "The Peshmerga forces in our area were weak," Shakir Hassan, who had fled to the mountain, told Al Jazeera. "They did not fight much." The Kurdish regional president, Massoud Barzani, responded publicly that there must be no room for negligence and that measures would be taken against anyone who had been remiss in protecting people.

The UN human rights office and the UN mission in Iraq later wrote that the fleeing included Yazidis, Shia Turkmen, Shia Shabak and Christians. Many went north to the Sinjar mountain range, others to Dohuk in the Kurdish region. A rapid assessment cited in the UN report found that 25 percent of the district's population had reached the Kurdish region and 75 percent were still inside the district.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs put the number stuck around Sinjar at between 35,000 and 50,000 on 5 August. A week later CNN cited an estimate of 40,000 hiding in the mountains. A footnote in the UN report went much higher, saying up to 200,000 had sought refuge on the mountain, 75 percent of them Yazidi.

The conditions were harsh. People trapped there told Al Jazeera that as many as 30 had starved, mostly children, though the outlet said it could not verify the claim. UNICEF said on 5 August that about 40 children had died "as a direct consequence of violence, displacement and dehydration", and that up to 25,000 children were stranded and needed water and sanitation. The UN report quoted callers on the mountain who said more than 12 children had died on 3 August and two more, aged 5 and 3, on 4 August.

The Yazidi member of the Iraqi parliament, Vian Dakhil, was the community's most visible voice. In a tearful speech she told lawmakers that 70 Yazidi children had died, that women were being killed or enslaved and that 500 men had been "slaughtered". "There is a collective attempt to exterminate the Yazidi people," she said, according to CNN. Those figures were her account, and the UNICEF count differed from hers. Witnesses also told UN staff that some women jumped from the mountain with their children, out of desperation.

The Iraqi Air Force dropped food and relief on 4 and 5 August, according to the UN report, but people on the mountain told UN staff the supplies missed their targets and were not enough. Al Jazeera's Yazidi sources said some of the aid was ruined because helicopters flew high to avoid being shot down. On 12 August an Iraqi helicopter delivering aid crashed after picking up about two dozen Yazidis; the pilot died. Survivors included Dakhil and a New York Times correspondent, CNN reported, and the Kurdish government's chief of staff said the cause appeared to be pilot error while the military cited a technical failure.

The UN report is the most detailed record in the pages used here. It says staff received numerous reports of serious, systematic abuses against Yazidi civilians on 2 and 3 August. It lists accounts, each attributed to witnesses, survivors or community leaders and often unverified:

On 3 August, IS fighters reportedly chased ten Yazidi families fleeing the al-Qahtaniya area, killing the men and abducting the women and children. On 4 August they reportedly killed 60 men from Hardan village and took their wives and daughters, allegedly to Tal Afar. Yazidi community leaders said on 4 August that at least 200 Yazidis had been killed in Sinjar and 60 to 70 more in the Ramadi Jabal area, and that at least 50 women had been abducted from Tal Binat.

People who reached safety described mass killings between 3 and 6 August. Among the accounts the report recorded: more than 50 bodies showing signs of torture near Dhola village; about 100 killed in Khana Sor; 250 to 300 killed in the Hardan area, at least ten of them beheaded, after IS reportedly promised them safety if they gave up their weapons; and more than 200 killed by mortar fire on the road between Adnaniya and Jazeera. Survivors said that at Qiniyeh village, which has a water source, fighters separated men, women and children, took their belongings and shot 70 to 90 men in a ditch. Amnesty International told CNN that one relative described more than 30 members of two families from Khana Sor killed or abducted.

The worst single account in the report concerns Khocho. Residents had told the UN their village was under siege and that they had been told to convert or die. Five survivors said that on 15 August fighters gathered every male over the age of ten at the school, drove them out of the village and shot them: as many as 400, they estimated. Dozens of women and children were abducted, possibly as many as 1,000, they said, and were taken to Tal Afar. On 24 and 25 August, according to witnesses, fourteen elderly Yazidi men were executed at the Sheikh Mand shrine near Jidala and the shrine was blown up.

The UN also recorded reports, which it described as unverified, that women had been forced to convert and marry fighters, or held as war booty or sold as slaves. Iraq's human rights minister Sudani told Reuters on 10 August that the government had "striking evidence" including crime scene images that at least 500 Yazidis had been executed, that some victims, including women and children, were buried alive, and that about 300 women were taken as slaves. Journalists could not enter IS-held areas, Al Jazeera noted, so many early claims could not be independently confirmed.

The plight of the Yazidis and the IS push against the Kurdish region prompted the United States to begin targeted air strikes, CNN reported. President Barack Obama approved them on a Friday and strikes hit IS positions in the Sinjar area on Saturday 9 August, according to the Guardian. The BBC later listed the Sinjar attack among the reasons for the US air campaign, which reached Syria the following month. An RAF transport aircraft made the first British airdrop of humanitarian aid on the mountain on the Saturday night, joining the US in dropping water, filtration devices, food and tents, the Guardian said. On 12 August the US defense secretary, Chuck Hagel, said about 130 Marines and special operations personnel were being sent to Irbil, adding: "this is not a combat boots on the ground operation."

By 10 August people were coming down. A Kurdish official at the Fishkhabur crossing, Shawkat Barbahari, said peshmerga had escorted 30,000 Yazidis through Syria and back into Kurdistan, while a UN spokesman reported 15,000 to 20,000 and said the UN was not directly involved and could not confirm the numbers. Dakhil put it at 20,000 to 30,000. The UN report, drawing on the humanitarian office, said that since 6 August around 80,000 displaced people from Sinjar District, mostly Yazidi, had crossed into the Kurdish region.

Not everyone got out. In mid-December about 8,000 Kurdish peshmerga, backed by 45 coalition air strikes according to the BBC, advanced from Zumar towards the mountain. Masrour Barzani, head of the Kurdish region's security council, said on 18 December that the siege was broken and that all the Yazidis trapped there were free; DW reported the same statement. Kurdish officials said about 80 militants died according to the BBC, and 100 according to Barzani as quoted by DW. The BBC's correspondent cautioned that the objective was limited and that Sinjar town, further south, was still vulnerable.

On 21 March, five years after the attack, the UN investigative team UNITAD, set up under Security Council resolution 2379 (2017) to collect evidence of crimes by IS, announced that it had completed the opening of its first Yazidi grave in the Sinjar region, at the village of Kojo. The work took five days, with Iraqi and Kurdish forensic teams, and exposed the remains of up to 30 people. The final number was to be set by forensic analysis in Baghdad.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nadia Murad, a survivor of the massacre and mass abductions at Kojo, spoke at a memorial ceremony. UNITAD's head, Karim Khan, told the community: "You have already waited a long time. And I'm sorry to say you will have to wait longer. Because the road to real justice is a long one." He said the crimes "may amount to genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity", wording that left the legal finding to later proceedings.
